newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian latex demand to moderate in new decade.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian latex demand to moderate in new decade.

text.p: Malaysia, the world's largest producer and user of latex, is expected to see local demand for the rubber raw material moderating in the next decade, an industry seminar heard on Monday.

Consumption of latex concentrate is expected to grow slowly over the next five years to 270,000 tonnes in 2000 from 242,522 tonnes in 1995, S.K. Koh, a senior researcher with the Malaysian Rubber Research and Development Board (MRRDB), said.
Domestic demand of 300,000 tonnes has been forecast by the year 2005, she told the seminar on changes and development in Malaysia's latex-based industry.

"The double-digit growth experienced in the Malaysian rubber products sector in the last decade is not expected to continue indefinitely," Koh said. "The future path of the industry will be determined by several factors, both external and domestic."

After benefiting immensely from a global-wide jump in usage of condoms and surgical gloves in 1988 due to the AIDS scare, the Malaysian latex products industry has stagnated from competition from other rubber producing countries.
Malaysia's latex production fell to 249,200 tonnes in 1995 from a high of 304,000 tonnes in 1993. Exports fell to 108,700 tonnes last year from 120,600 in 1993.

"In the international market, the competitiveness of Malaysian-made latex products has to contend with...producers located in NR (natural rubber) producing countries such as Thailand, Indonesia, India and China," Koh said.

"Newly-emerging countries like Vietnam, Cambodia, Myanmar (Burma) are also potential producers to watch. These countries have the advantage of abundant labour resources as well as supply of raw materials," Koh added.
Long-term feasiblity also depends on cost-competitiveness and raw material supply, she said.

Malaysian rubber products makers were already relocating to other countries. The growing cost of labour and infrastructural inputs, together with convenience of raw material supply outside, would ensure this continues, she said.
Another factor is the impending increase in latex-processing costs due to tougher waste disposal laws in Malaysia, said Koh.

Abdul Halim Hassan, another MRRDB senior researcher, said the proposed Standard Malaysian Glove scheme will be a positive factor for the latex industry in the future. The scheme aims to distinguish Malaysian gloves from others in terms of quality.

In addition the merger of the MRRDB and two other bodies -- the Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board and the Rubber Research Institute of Malaysia -- will be a catalyst to future downstream activities, he added. --Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-2307509)
